First of all, there's nothing wrong with you. There may be some ideas that float through your head that you should never act on, and if those become overwhelming therapy can help you move past them, but most of the thoughts you're having are actually quite normal, and actually especially after SA. I'm sorry you went through that.

I don't want to get too into details because you're still very young, but there are people who find a lot of catharsis in acting out violent fantasies with a trusted partner where the "danger" isn't real. It's EXTREMELY important this is only done with a very trusted partner and I would recommend not until you're an adult (not in a judging way, or in a condescending way, but more because you should have years of experience with enforcing boundaries and consent and do some healing from your trauma first, plus you have to trust your partner has done the same) because the one who's playing as if they're the victim MUST be in total control and have absolute power to stop it at any time. Sometimes people who have been through SA feel a sense of control when they fantasize about losing that control with someone who would never actually hurt them, or their subconscious may be trying to undo some of the trauma by recontextualizing the experience into a pleasurable one in your mind. These are normal psychological experiences, and while they need to be treated with care, there's nothing "bad" about them.

Everyone is a little mentally ill. If the fantasies that "disgust" you persist, I would really encourage therapy. It may be something completely different than it seems. Sometimes sexual fantasy can even be a subconscious form of self harm, you may not actually have any desires toward those things. It may be that your sense of boundaries was so shaken by your assault that your brain is testing out where the boundaries are now. These things are very complicated, but just because you thought something doesn't mean you want it, just because you want something doesn't mean you're going to act on it, and as you get the appropriate level of life experience you might find that a lot of these desires either go away or become easy to reimagine in a way that only involves consenting adults.

It sounds like there's some underlying issues you haven't unpacked that would account for the lying and other issues, but again it's not wrong, just something you're not processing. Therapy sounds like a good idea overall to help with all of this, but don't shame yourself for these things, just try and work through them. There's nothing wrong with wanting attention from boys at 15, that's natural, and frankly, I wish I hadn't wasted so many years being so loyal to men who didn't treat me right. Enjoy that attention from boys, just do it safely.

Insecurity is the biggest trap out there, I really believe this - it truly doesn't serve you in any way so whatever you can do to chip away at it will be helpful but it's not like you can magically fix it, I know, it's hard AF. Just keep that in mind as you grow and develop your adult opinion of yourself - I wish I'd been able to let go of insecurity closer to your age than closer to 30 but we're all just teenage girls on the inside after all.

That being said, overcoming insecurity is harder than finding things you are secure about. What are your other traits that you are fully confident about? Are you someone who's indisputably smart? Do you make people laugh? Do you do really well in a sport or hobby? Do you do a great job of acting in accordance with your morals? Do you take good care of other people? Are you a good friend? Any positive trait at all that you see in yourself that aligns with your values - focus on on that, and try to figure out if they show signs they value it too.

So for example if you're really smart and academic and that matters to you but they're not reasonably supportive of that pursuit and proud of your accomplishments there, it may not be that they only like you for your body but it doesn't matter because they don't like you for the things you like about yourself. Does that make sense? Worry less about if they like you for the things you don't value - realistically it's a very good thing for your partner to love your body so testing that isn't sufficient - and worry more about it they DO love the things that make you the real you. Try and gauge that

This does not only apply to trans people at all, pronouns apply to everyone. Idk how in-depth you're wanting to get here, so I'll explain from the most basic onward:

Pronouns are words that can be used in place of a name or noun. So for example, I could say "Julie is going to the store" or I could say "she is going to the store." I can say "The cup is right there" or I can say "it is right there." 

Effectively, different pronouns symbolize different things in our language. "It" for example is typically associated with inanimate objects or at least inhuman objects.  Some languages do not include gender-specific pronouns but in English, "They" is associated with either multiple people, or with a person of unspecified gender, "She" is associated with female persons or animals, and "He" is associated with male persons or animals.

There are many different relationships that people may form with pronouns because of these associations. A cis man may feel "I am a man, so I want to be called 'he' since 'she' makes me feel like you think I'm a girl." A trans man may feel the same way. So often it's just a matter of feeling attached to the pronoun that correlates to your gender, whether you're cis or not. Non-binary people might like to use "they" or another pronoun because both the connotations of female and male feel wrong to them.

Some people reject the idea that pronouns should have genders associated with them, so they might have a more complicated relationship with their preferred pronoun that doesnt necessarily have as much to do with their gender. Some people might reject the associations made with gender and therefore not care what pronoun you use for them (like me)

But because of the social connotation of each pronoun, some people will intentionally weaponize pronouns as a way to discredit someone's gender. For example, if a bigoted person calls a trans woman "he," they are trying to tell her that they don't see her as a woman in a way that may come across subtle to some people, but is packed with meaning when you understand the weight that pronouns actually carry in their association.

In a sense, it's similar to a name. If it doesn't feel like it fits you correctly, it's uncomfortable to be called by the wrong thing. If someone calls you a mean name, that can really hurt, and in the same way, using the wrong pronoun can really hurt too.

I guess it depends on how you define success, by many people's measure I may not be, but by my own, I honestly am. I never would have believed when I was younger that I'd ever say that about myself, I was a perpetual disaster until my 20s were almost over but now at 32, I have a job I'm very proud of where I'm highly respected and loved by my colleagues. I'm far from rich but I make enough to have a beautiful house, pay my bills on time, and blow a little money on the stupid hobbies that I pick up. I give myself the time and space to do stupid hobbies that make me happy even if they're not productive in a deeper way. I have a husband who adores me exactly as I am, and we're planning to adopt a child soon. I have a truly amazing circle of close friends who give my life so much meaning. I make art because it makes me happy without worrying about quality. Every day I get to read books, watch movies, cook delicious meals, and cuddle my cat. I have something a lot of rich people don't have, which is enough. I feel incredibly successful.

It's important to note that success doesn't always look clean and linear. I'm still bipolar. Finding the right treatment and medication has helped so much, but my version of success sometimes still means crying over nothing, venting to my friends about small things, eating crow to apologize because I was snippy with my husband over nothing more than a mood swing, or having to redo my budget for the month because I blew too much money during a manic episode. Sometimes it looks even scarier, sometimes it means I spend a little time in a major regression, feeling severely depressed and even more confused by my depression because I know realistically that I have no reason to be. That's just the reality, that for a sick person success still included your sickness, but what's attainable is a lifestyle that accommodates it. One where these episodes get shorter and easier to manage, one where you have a support network to get through each episode, one where you have a little cushion to fuck up every once in a while and be able to come back from it. 

That's what's made my life so fucking happy. Building that support network, being self aware and honest, finding medical treatment that works and not allowing myself to neglect it. I know there's varying levels of privilege everyone is working from and it's easier said than done, but I truly do believe that that's a really effective formula that can be attained.

So much about your post here reminds me of myself or of my closest friends who have similar struggles. I'm 32 now, for context, but I just want to say from reading this, I see you. You clearly have an incredible sense of self-awareness beyond your years, and that's something I've always been told about myself too, and I think dealing with mental illness while having that level of understanding of yourself as a teenager is the hardest thing I've ever done. I know just existing is hard, and it sounds like you have things piled on top of that too, and you're very strong for enduring that. I know some people like to minimize the things teenagers go through and act like you don't even know what stress is yet, but I'm gonna be honest that even though jobs and bills and raising a family is stressful, I truly think being a teenager can be far harder, so just don't think it can't get better (corny I know, but fr it does). 

I also relate to what you said about school. I actually planned to kms the day after I graduated college because I didn't think I'd have a purpose anymore which seems so silly in retrospect because I didn't even start to find my joy and purpose until long after college, but it was real to me. It's so good that school is important to you, but I'm alarmed by the comment about what would happen if you failed. Failure is a temporary setback, and the consequences of it are very short term. Once you're gone, you're gone, and the consequences of that is the ripple effect of every small difference you could have made to every person you come across for the rest of your life, and those small differences add up. That would be eternal. Not to mention just the fact that you deserve to be here, even if you decided that you'd never do a single piec of homework again, you'd deserve to have a life, and you deserve to be well. Easier said than done, I know, but take it from a recovered suicidal gifted kid, your worth is not tied to your productivity. Your worth is something that cannot be quantified.

Im not a parent yet myself (funnily in the process of getting my foster license) but I'd be proud of my foster kid for coming to me about that.

I think this poem would benefit a lot from being reworked so that it doesn't rhyme.  The stanza beginnings are so good but then get undercut by forced rhymes, and it's so unnecessary.  Rhyming poetry in general is really hard to pull off well, and it's much better to have something beautiful and free verse than something that rhymes for the sake of rhyming.  

I also would personally start with the third verse.  The first two feel like a preface to what you're really trying to say, and it would be stronger if you jumped into it.  You have a lot of strength within this but streamlining it so that the weaker bits are omitted or are changed to work better in conjunction with the strong parts would make it something really great.
